claim: The study developed an approach combining commercially available automated phenotyping hardware with a systems biology analysis pipeline to generate high-dimensional readout of mouse behavior and physiology.
source: To address this, we developed an approach that combines commercially available automated phenotyping hardware with a systems biology analysis pipeline to generate a high-dimensional readout of mouse behavior/physiology, as well as intuitive and health-relevant summary statistics (resilience and biological age).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a methodological development of the study.

claim: The platform was used to longitudinally evaluate aging in hundreds of outbred mice across an age range from 3 months to 3.4 years.
source: We used this platform to longitudinally evaluate aging in hundreds of outbred mice across an age range from 3 months to 3.4 years.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract describing the study design.

claim: Widespread physiological and behavioral aging was observed starting in early life, contrary to the assumption that aging can only be measured at the limits of animal ability via challenge-based tasks.
source: In contrast to the assumption that aging can only be measured at the limits of animal ability via challenge-based tasks, we observed widespread physiological and behavioral aging starting in early life.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract, contrasting with previous assumptions.

claim: Organism-level resilience exhibited an accelerating decline with age that was distinct from the trajectory of individual phenotypes.
source: Using network connectivity analysis, we found that organism-level resilience exhibited an accelerating decline with age that was distinct from the trajectory of individual phenotypes.
evidence: This finding is explicitly stated in the abstract as a result of network connectivity analysis.

claim: The CASPAR method was developed for jointly predicting chronological age and survival time.
source: We developed a method, Combined Aging and Survival Prediction of Aging Rate (CASPAR), for jointly predicting chronological age and survival time and showed that the resulting model is able to predict both variables simultaneously, a behavior that is not captured by separate age and mortality prediction models.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a methodological development.

claim: The CASPAR model is able to predict both chronological age and survival time simultaneously, a behavior not captured by separate age and mortality prediction models.
source: We developed a method, Combined Aging and Survival Prediction of Aging Rate (CASPAR), for jointly predicting chronological age and survival time and showed that the resulting model is able to predict both variables simultaneously, a behavior that is not captured by separate age and mortality prediction models.
evidence: This is a key finding about the CASPAR model stated in the abstract.

claim: The laboratory mouse is commonly used to study aging and test putative aging interventions.
source: The laboratory mouse is commonly used to study aging and test putative aging interventions (Ackert-Bicknell et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Lifespan in mice is not necessarily the best criterion for assessing the efficacy of aging interventions or for evaluating their potential translation to humans.
source: While many studies have used lifespan extension as an endpoint, lifespan in mice is not necessarily the best criterion for assessing the efficacy of aging interventions or for evaluating their potential translation to humans; measuring health is an important additional source of information (Hansen and Kennedy, 2016; Fischer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Health is a multi-parameter, organism-level state.
source: Health is a multi-parameter, organism-level state, and as multiple aspects of health decline with age, a sophisticated assessment of aging and putative aging interventions should evaluate as many organism-level aspects of health as possible (Freund, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Many challenge-based assays are labor- and time-intensive, limiting the number that any one study can include.
source: However, many of these assays are labor- and time-intensive, thus the number that any one study can include is limited.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a limitation of existing methods.

claim: Challenge-based assays have limited repeatability due to stress on animals and changes in performance due to training, reducing their utility for longitudinal analysis.
source: Further, these assays often utilize a challenge, for example, performance on a difficult task, and due to the stress this places on the animals as well as changes in performance due to training, challenge-based assays have limited repeatability, reducing their utility for longitudinal analysis (Huffman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Many assays are highly operator-dependent, adversely impacting reproducibility.
source: Lastly, many assays are highly operator-dependent, adversely impacting reproducibility (Brown et al., 2018; Voelkl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The study utilized commercially available, automated monitoring cages that simultaneously and continuously record physiological and behavioral parameters.
source: To develop an alternative approach, we utilized commercially available, automated monitoring cages that simultaneously and continuously record physiological and behavioral parameters (voluntary animal position, respiration, weight, food and water intake, and wheel activity) (Brown et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the methodology.

claim: Each sensor in the cage provides dense time series data, with time windows ranging from <1 s (photobeam breaks) to 3 min (gas measurements).
source: Each of the sensors in the cage provides dense time series data, with time windows ranging from <1 s (photobeam breaks) to 3 min (gas measurements).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the data collection capabilities.

claim: The most common analytical approach for automated cage data is to average data into 12 hr time bins (dark and light phase).
source: The most common analytical approach is to average this data into 12 hr time bins, that is, dark and light phase.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing current analytical practices.

claim: Generating hundreds of features from raw data streams allows insights into behavior and physiology to be uncovered via tools such as network modeling.
source: We hypothesized that, by generating hundreds of features from these raw data streams, insights into behavior and physiology could be uncovered via tools such as network modeling, which have previously been restricted to lower levels of biological organization.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a hypothesis of the study.

claim: Automated phenotyping removes confounders such as operator-induced variability, increasing data robustness.
source: Further, automated phenotyping removes confounders such as operator-induced variability, increasing data robustness (Chesler et al., 2002a).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The study used the diversity outbred (DO) population, a heterogeneous stock derived from the intercrossing of eight inbred founder strains, in which each mouse is genetically unique.
source: We used this platform to assess aging in the diversity outbred (DO) population, a heterogeneous stock derived from the intercrossing of eight inbred founder strains, in which each mouse is genetically unique (Churchill et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Phenotype and intervention response are highly dependent on genetic background, meaning findings in one mouse strain may not generalize to other mouse strains or humans.
source: Phenotype and intervention response are highly dependent on genetic background, meaning that the findings in one mouse strain may not generalize to other mouse strains, let alone to humans (Voelkl et al., 2020; Sittig et al., 2016; Mandillo et al., 2008; Kafkafi et al., 2018; Tuttle et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Genetic diversity introduces inter-individual variation, which is useful when building networks based on phenotypic correlations.
source: Second, genetic diversity introduces inter-individual variation, which is useful when building networks based on phenotypic correlations.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an advantage of using genetically diverse mice.

claim: Genetic diversity introduces deliberate biological variation to increase the external validity of study findings.
source: Third, and perhaps most importantly, genetic diversity introduces deliberate biological variation in order to increase the external validity of study findings (Voelkl et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The study generated approximately 60 years of data across 415 female DO mice, from an age range of 6 weeks to 40.5 months (3.4 years).
source: We generated ~60 years of data across 415 female DO mice, from an age range of 6 weeks to 40.5 months (3.4 years).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the scope of the dataset.

claim: The study utilized a staggered enrollment design in which mice were enrolled at different ages, between 3 and 24 months.
source: We utilized a staggered enrollment design in which mice were enrolled at different ages, between 3 and 24 months, to ensure that the dataset contains hundreds of runs for all age groups up to 30+ months of age, providing consistent statistical power across an average mouse lifespan.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the study design.

claim: This represents the highest-resolution assessment of murine physiological aging to date, examining animals monthly whereas previous assessments sampled animals in ≥6-month intervals.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the highest-resolution assessment of murine physiological aging to date: we examined animals monthly, whereas previous assessments of physiological aging sampled animals in ≥6-month intervals (Ladiges et al., 2017; Fischer et al., 2016; Petr et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations comparing to previous work.

claim: High-resolution phenotyping was manageable because the passive monitoring platform required only 20 hr of hands-on time per week from a single operator.
source: High-resolution phenotyping was manageable because our passive monitoring platform required only 20 hr of hands-on time per week from a single operator; as we and others have experienced, challenge-based phenotyping pipelines require so much hands-on time and often place such stress on the animals that they cannot be repeated frequently.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction describing the practical advantages of the approach.

claim: The platform detected hundreds of aging-related changes starting early in life, demonstrating that passive monitoring has the sensitivity to quantify aging even in a highly variable strain background.
source: The platform detected hundreds of aging-related changes starting early in life, demonstrating that this passive monitoring approach has the sensitivity to quantify aging even in a highly variable strain background.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding of the study.

claim: Network analysis demonstrated that different behavioral and physiological clusters exhibited distinct aging dynamics.
source: Network analysis demonstrated that different behavioral and physiological clusters exhibited distinct aging dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding from network analysis.

claim: Resilience exhibited an accelerating decline that was distinct from any individual phenotype.
source: By employing analytical methods to measure overall network connectivity, we quantified resilience, an emergent property, and found that it exhibited an accelerating decline that was distinct from any individual phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a key finding about resilience.

claim: The study builds upon pre-existing literature from other model organisms, particularly nematodes, demonstrating that passive, automated monitoring can be used to quantify multi-dimensional, organism-level aging.
source: Our study builds upon pre-existing literature from other model organisms, particularly nematodes, demonstrating that passive, automated monitoring can be used to quantify multi-dimensional, organism-level aging (Zhang et al., 2016; Le et al., 2020; Martineau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The study constructed a system of 64 semi-automated phenotyping cages that continuously measured multiple aspects of mouse physiology and behavior.
source: To test this idea, we constructed a system of 64 semi-automated phenotyping cages that continuously measured multiple aspects of mouse physiology and behavior (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Cages record oxygen and carbon dioxide concentration, water vapor, weight of food and water hoppers, mouse body mass, running wheel rotations, and mouse position via a three-dimensional array of infrared beams.
source: Cages record oxygen and carbon dioxide concentration, water vapor, weight of food and water hoppers, mouse body mass (when inside the sleeping chamber), running wheel rotations, and mouse position via a three-dimensional array of infrared beams.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the measurement capabilities.

claim: Gas measurements are acquired every 3 min because the time constant of the cage only allows for meaningful changes in gas concentrations every ~3 min.
source: Gas measurements are acquired every 3 min because the time constant of the cage (rate at which air is replaced) only allows for meaningful changes in gas concentrations every ~3 min.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the measurement frequency.

claim: Other measurements (besides gas) are acquired every second.
source: Other measurements are acquired every second.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing measurement frequency.

claim: Each mouse was monitored for 1 week per month.
source: We chose to monitor each mouse for 1 week per month (Figure 1B), as we reasoned that (1) a 7-day run would provide enough data for a robust and stable estimation of physiological/behavioral status and (2) monthly rotations would be sufficiently granular to capture the pace of aging in mice.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The monitoring schedule allowed regular monitoring of fourfold as many animals as there were cages (256 animals with 64 cages).
source: This schedule allowed us to regularly monitor fourfold as many animals as we had cages, that is, 256.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the study design.

claim: The same animal was placed in different cages for different runs to mitigate any cage-specific measurement effects.
source: We placed the same animal in different cages for different runs, to mitigate any cage-specific measurement effects.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental design.

claim: The study initially enrolled 256 female DO mice split among four age groups (n = 64 at 7, 14, 21, and 25 months).
source: We initially enrolled 256 female DO mice (Churchill et al., 2012) split among four age groups (n = 64 at 7, 14, 21, and 25 months), and we enrolled younger (~3 months) animals in semi-regular waves as the older cohorts expired.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the study cohort.

claim: Enrolling animals at different ages ensured that different ages were similarly represented and mitigated the loss of power that occurs with time due to mortality.
source: Enrolling animals at different ages ensured that different ages were similarly represented and mitigated the loss of power that occurs with time due to mortality.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the rationale for the study design.

claim: Enrolling animals at different calendar dates ensured that age and calendar date were not perfectly correlated, attenuating the effect of any unknown environmental effects.
source: Enrolling animals at different calendar dates ensured that age and calendar date were not perfectly correlated, attenuating the effect of any unknown, but potentially confounding, environmental effects such as seasonal changes or temperature drift over time.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the rationale for the study design.

claim: The study utilized DO mice to avoid strain-specific results that would be less likely to generalize.
source: We utilized DO mice in order to avoid strain-specific results that would be less likely to generalize; however, as a practical necessity, we only examined female mice in this study.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the choice of mouse strain.

claim: In total, 415 animals were enrolled.
source: In total, we enrolled 415 animals, with an age distribution that provided large numbers of animals at both young and old ages (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The study was run for approximately 1.5 years, during which 212 mice died (51%) and 203 mice were censored at the end of the study (49%).
source: The study was run for approximately 1.5 years, during which 212 mice died (51%) and 203 mice were censored at the end of the study (49%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the study outcomes.

claim: DO mice had a median lifespan of 25 months (~2 years) and a maximal lifespan of 41 months (~3.4 years).
source: Accounting for truncation and censoring, DO mice had a median lifespan of 25 months (~2 years) and a maximal lifespan of 41 months (~3.4 years) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: After quality control filtering, the study obtained data for 3143 7-day runs, representing approximately 60 years of dense time series data.
source: In total, after quality control filtering, we obtained data for 3143 7-day runs, that is, ~60 years of dense time series data, from an age range of 6 weeks to 40.5 months (3.4 years), with virtually all ages containing data from multiple cohorts (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1D.

claim: DO mice have a broad body mass distribution, ranging from 15 to 60 g.
source: Indeed, we found a broad body mass distribution in this cohort, ranging from 15 to 60 g (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There is a highly significant positive correlation between body mass and energy expenditure in this dataset.
source: We compared body mass to energy expenditure (kcal/hr) in this dataset and saw a highly significant correlation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: For all gas-derived measurements except RQ, the study normalized for body mass via linear regression.
source: As we already had body mass information, we were primarily interested in changes to energy expenditure and related parameters that were body mass independent, therefore for all gas-derived measurements except RQ (VO2, VCO2, VH2O, and energy expenditure), because it is a ratio, we normalized for body mass via linear regression.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing data processing.

claim: Body mass correction removed the positive correlation between body mass and energy expenditure.
source: This removed the positive correlation with body mass (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The study developed a data processing pipeline that provides aggregated, quality-controlled data at various levels of resolution.
source: We developed a data processing pipeline that provides aggregated, quality-controlled data at various levels of resolution (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Data are initially processed into 14 'base features' in 3 min bins.
source: Initially, data are processed into 14 'base features' in 3 min bins: BodyMass (weight), Food (food intake), Water (water intake), WheelMeters (distance traveled on wheel), PedMeters (distance traveled in cage), AllMeters (PedMeters + fine motor movements), XBreak (number of photobeam breaks in the X axis), YBreak (number of photobeam breaks in the Y axis), ZBreak (number of photobeam breaks in the vertical axis), VO2 (oxygen consumption), VCO2 (carbon dioxide production), energy expenditure (kcal/hr), RQ (respiratory quotient − VCO2/VO2), VH2O (water vapor).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the data processing pipeline.

claim: Animals exhibited circadian patterns of behavior and physiology, with increased activity during the dark phase.
source: As expected, animals exhibited circadian patterns of behavior and physiology, with increased activity during the dark phase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing observed patterns.

claim: Clear aging-related changes were observed for most of the 14 base features, starting from the youngest ages examined.
source: Clear aging-related change were observed for most of the 14 base features, starting from the youngest ages we examined.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a key finding.

claim: Animals exhibited a concave body mass trajectory: gaining weight until 21–24 months of age, then progressively losing weight.
source: One of the most striking changes we observed was a concave body mass trajectory: animals gained weight until 21–24 months of age, then progressively lost weight (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There was a significant decline in wheel running, food intake, water intake, mass-adjusted energy expenditure, and rate of whole-body water loss (VH2O) with age.
source: Other striking changes included a significant decline in wheel running, food intake, water intake, and a decline in mass-adjusted energy expenditure and rate of whole-body water loss (VH2O) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: It has been previously reported that body weight declines in older mice despite a decrease in energy expenditure.
source: Consistent with these observations, it has been previously reported that body weight declines in older mice despite a decrease in energy expenditure (Petr et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Ambulatory activity (PedMeters, AllMeters, and YBreaks) tended to increase with age.
source: Not all base features declined with age – ambulatory activity (PedMeters, AllMeters, and YBreaks) tended to increase with age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: None of the aging-related changes mirrored the concave trajectory of body mass, demonstrating that multiple aging-related changes to physiology and behavior are not driven solely by weight changes.
source: None of these changes mirrored the concave trajectory of body mass, demonstrating that multiple aging-related changes to physiology and behavior are not driven solely by weight changes.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: The study fit a robust hidden Markov model (HMM) that uses base features to classify each 3 min time window into one of six states.
source: To quantify behavior, we fit a robust hidden Markov model (HMM) that uses base features of the phenotyping cages, excluding body mass, to classify each 3 min time window into one of six states.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analytical method.

claim: Each HMM state was characterized by a distinct combination of base features.
source: Each state was characterized by a distinct combination of base features (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), and we named the states Sleep, Rest, Eat, Eat&Drink, Run, and Active based on our qualitative interpretation of those patterns.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mice organized their behavior around the light cycle, with sharp transitions at lights on/off.
source: As expected, mice organized their behavior around the light cycle, with sharp transitions at lights on/off.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing observed patterns.

claim: Mice spent the vast majority of the light phase in lower activity states, whereas high activity state occupancy increased in the dark phase.
source: They spent the vast majority of the light phase in lower activity states, whereas high activity state occupancy increased in the dark phase (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Compared to young mice, old mice spent more time in low activity states during both light and dark phases.
source: There were differences in overall state occupancy between young (3–6 months) and old (30–33 months) mice; compared to young mice, old mice spent more time in low activity states (Figure 2C). This was true during both light and dark phases, though it was particularly obvious during the dark phase, where old mice spent far less time Running or Active than young mice and more time in the other four, lower activity, states.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Young animals spent nearly 70% of their time Running or Active during the early part of the dark phase, about 2 hr after lights off.
source: During this time, young animals spent nearly 70% of their time Running or Active.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing temporal patterns of behavior.

claim: Older animals exhibited their highest activity during the early dark phase, but their peak activity was much lower than young mice, and their transition to high activity when the lights initially turned off was slower.
source: Older animals also exhibited their highest activity during this time, but their peak activity was much lower than young mice, and their transition to high activity when the lights initially turned off was slower.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing age-related differences in behavior.

claim: Animals spent most of their time in mid-level activity states (Eat and Eat&Drink) near the light/dark transitions.
source: Mid-level activity states, that is, Eat and Eat&Drink, exhibited a different pattern: animals spent most of their time in these states near the light/dark transitions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing temporal patterns of behavior.

claim: At the end of the dark phase, there was a large increase in food and water intake, likely indicating that animals were 'stocking up' before the low-activity light phase.
source: At the end of the dark phase, in particular, this corresponded to a large increase in food and water intake (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), likely indicating that the animals were 'stocking up' before the low-activity light phase.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Prior to the large increase in food and water intake at the end of the dark phase, animals reached a dark phase minimum for food/water intake and a maximum for Sleep and Rest, indicating they took a nap.
source: Prior to this large increase in food and water intake, animals reached a dark phase minimum for food/water intake and a maximum for Sleep and Rest, that is, they took a nap.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing temporal patterns of behavior.

claim: Napping behavior exhibited different aging dynamics than the decline in high activity: whereas Run and Active declined until ~24 months of age, napping increased in frequency until ~18 months and then stabilized.
source: Napping behavior exhibited different aging dynamics than the decline in high activity noted above; whereas Run and Active declined until ~24 months of age, napping increased in frequency until ~18 months and then stabilized (see Rest during dark phase time windows, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Old animals were more entrained to the light cycle than young animals: young animals reached their peak Eat and Eat&Drink occupancy 1 hr after the lights turned on, whereas older animals reached their peak in the hour prior to lights on.
source: However, we found that old animals were actually more entrained to the light cycle than young animals: young animals reached their peak Eat and Eat&Drink occupancy 1 hr after the lights turned on, during what is generally considered the low activity, 'sleep' phase of the circadian cycle (Figure 2D). In contrast, older animals reached their peak Eat and Eat&Drink occupancy in the hour prior to lights on, then quickly transitioned to Sleep and Rest once the lights turned on.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: This increased entrainment of feeding behavior to the light cycle with age represents an aging-related circadian shift that has not been previously described.
source: Whatever the causal chain, this increased entrainment of feeding behavior to the light cycle with age represents an aging-related circadian shift that, to our knowledge, has not been previously described.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a novel finding.

claim: Overall sleep duration did not change with age.
source: Irrespective of age, all mice reached a peak Sleep occupancy of ~50% in the middle of the light phase, and overall sleep duration did not change with age (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: In young mice, periods of continuous sleep averaged 1.1 hr in duration; this declined quickly with age, plateauing at ~0.6 hr by 9–12 months of age, representing a 30 min reduction in the duration of an average sleep period.
source: In young mice, periods of continuous sleep averaged 1.1 hr in duration; this declined quickly with age, plateauing at ~0.6 hr by 9–12 months of age, representing a 30 min reduction in the duration of an average sleep period (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The number of sleeping periods increased with age, representing increased sleep fragmentation.
source: At the same time, number of sleeping periods increased with age, representing increased sleep fragmentation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing sleep patterns.

claim: The average duration of feeding periods increased with age while number of feeding periods decreased, representing a consolidation of feeding behavior.
source: In contrast, the average duration of feeding periods increased with age while number of feeding periods decreased (Figure 2F), representing a consolidation of feeding behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Increased food spilling has been reported in aging mice, which may result in old mice requiring more time than young mice to ingest an equal quantity of food and may explain the extended duration of feeding periods with age.
source: Increased food spilling has been reported in aging mice (Starr and Saito, 2012); this may result in old mice requiring more time than young mice to ingest an equal quantity of food and may explain the extended duration of feeding periods with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation and inference.

claim: The decline in overall mass-adjusted energy expenditure was, at least partly, a decline in resting metabolic rate – mice exhibited a decline in low-activity-state (Rest and Sleep) energy expenditure with age.
source: Examining energy expenditure while mice were resting demonstrated that the decline in overall mass-adjusted energy expenditure was, at least partly, a decline in resting metabolic rate – mice exhibited a decline in low-activity-state (Rest and Sleep) energy expenditure with age (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Energy expenditure during high activity states (Run and Active) was decreased with age, indicating reduced activity intensity.
source: Energy expenditure during high activity states (Run and Active) was also decreased, indicating reduced activity intensity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing energy expenditure patterns.

claim: Animals ran more slowly as they aged throughout most of life.
source: Consistent with this, animals ran more slowly as they aged throughout most of life (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Animals exhibited an aging-related decline in mass-adjusted VH2O (whole-body water loss rate) during all states, including Rest and Sleep, suggesting this is a consequence of altered internal physiology rather than altered behavior.
source: Animals also exhibited a aging-related decline in mass-adjusted VH2O, that is, whole-body water loss rate, during all states, including Rest and Sleep (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D), suggesting that this is a consequence of altered internal physiology rather than altered behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: The decline in water loss rate precedes the decline in overall water intake, so reduced water intake does not explain this effect.
source: Interestingly, the decline in water loss rate precedes the decline in overall water intake (see Figure 2A), so reduced water intake does not explain this effect; it may instead represent aging-related changes in body composition, as lean and fat mass retain different amounts of water (Vu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Figure 2A and a supporting citation.

claim: The study generated 309 features from the raw data using different aggregation approaches.
source: In order to obtain a holistic view of aging patterns, we generated 309 features from the raw data using a number of different approaches
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing feature engineering.

claim: After multiple hypothesis correction, 244 features (79%) significantly changed with age.
source: After multiple hypothesis correction, 244 features (79%) significantly changed with age (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with reference to Supplementary file 1.

claim: Features exhibited a variety of trajectories and ages of onset, many of which were distinct from the base features, demonstrating that feature engineering uncovered additional physiological information.
source: Features exhibited a variety of trajectories and ages of onset (Figure 2G), many of which were distinct from the base features, demonstrating that feature engineering uncovered additional physiological information.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The diversity of aging patterns shows that passive phenotyping has the sensitivity to detect aging across the entire lifespan.
source: This diversity of aging patterns shows that (1) passive phenotyping has the sensitivity to detect aging across the entire lifespan and (2) physiological aging is more complex than simple linear trajectories and thus both dense time sampling and multi-dimensional phenotyping are needed to accurately capture the many different domains of physiological aging.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Physiological aging is more complex than simple linear trajectories and thus both dense time sampling and multi-dimensional phenotyping are needed to accurately capture the many different domains of physiological aging.
source: This diversity of aging patterns shows that (1) passive phenotyping has the sensitivity to detect aging across the entire lifespan and (2) physiological aging is more complex than simple linear trajectories and thus both dense time sampling and multi-dimensional phenotyping are needed to accurately capture the many different domains of physiological aging.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the data.

claim: Each animal in the DO population is genetically unique, allowing for estimation of the heritability and genetic architecture of traits.
source: Each animal in the DO population is genetically unique, allowing for estimation of the heritability and genetic architecture of traits.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the genetic analysis.

claim: Heritability analysis serves as a test of the biological validity of the different aggregation approaches, because only approaches that capture real biological signal should exhibit significant heritability.
source: This analysis serves as a test of the biological validity of the different aggregation approaches noted above, because only approaches that capture real biological signal should exhibit significant heritability.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the rationale for heritability analysis.

claim: Body mass exhibited high heritability (~30%).
source: As expected, body mass exhibited high heritability (~30%); body mass in DO mice has previously been shown to be highly heritable (Wright et al., 2020) and is largely invariant to state or time of day, hence high heritability across aggregation methods.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: At least some features derived from each of the aggregation approaches showed significant heritability.
source: Importantly, at least some features derived from each of the aggregation approaches showed significant heritability, and in many cases these state- or time-conditioned base features showed higher heritability than the same base feature averaged across the entire run (the 'overall' feature).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing heritability results.

claim: State- or time-conditioned base features often showed higher heritability than the same base feature averaged across the entire run.
source: Importantly, at least some features derived from each of the aggregation approaches showed significant heritability, and in many cases these state- or time-conditioned base features showed higher heritability than the same base feature averaged across the entire run (the 'overall' feature).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing heritability results.

claim: Heritability of X and Y breaks during the Eat&Drink state was higher than overall X and Y breaks.
source: For example, heritability of X and Y breaks during the Eat&Drink state was higher than overall X and Y breaks.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an example of heritability patterns.

claim: Different aggregation approaches capture biological information that is distinct from overall averages.
source: This suggests that the different aggregation approaches capture biological information that is distinct from overall averages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from heritability analysis.

claim: 33 features exhibited significant nonzero heritability (after removing body mass-derived features except overall body mass).
source: After removing all body mass-derived features except for overall body mass in order to avoid redundancy, 33 features exhibited significant nonzero heritability (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The four most heritable features, with heritabilities >30%, involved pedestrian locomotion (AllMeters, PedMeters, PedSpeed, Xbreaks, or YBreaks).
source: The four most heritable features, with heritabilities >30%, involved pedestrian locomotion (AllMeters, PedMeters, PedSpeed, Xbreaks, or YBreaks).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing heritability results.

claim: 17 out of 33 (52%) of significantly heritable features involved pedestrian locomotion, suggesting that animal movement is an aspect of behavior with a strong genetic component.
source: In total, 17/33 (52%) of significantly heritable features involved pedestrian locomotion, suggesting that animal movement is an aspect of behavior with a strong genetic component.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with inference from the data.

claim: The body mass-conditioned gas measurements mostly lacked significant heritability (or the heritability was below detection ability), suggesting that respiration, once accounting for body mass, is mostly influenced by environment rather than genetics.
source: Interestingly, aside from several energy expenditure-based features, the body mass-conditioned gas measurements mostly lacked significant heritability (or at least, the heritability was below our ability to detect), suggesting that respiration, once accounting for body mass, is mostly influenced by environment rather than genetics.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with inference from the data.

claim: Genetic correlations were, on average, stronger than phenotypic correlations (median genetic correlation = 0.22, median phenotypic correlation = 0.16).
source: We observed a large number of positive and negative genetic correlations; in fact, the genetic correlations were, on average, stronger than phenotypic correlations (median genetic correlation = 0.22, median phenotypic correlation = 0.16), which is reasonable if the different environmental contributions to a pair of phenotypes are mostly uncorrelated noise.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing genetic correlation analysis.

claim: The high degree of similarity between genetic and phenotypic correlations suggests that, in future studies, additional genetic mapping power could be attained by analyzing phenotypes jointly.
source: Further, the high degree of similarity between genetic and phenotypic correlations suggest that, in future studies, additional genetic mapping power could be attained by analyzing phenotypes jointly.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the genetic correlation analysis.

claim: The interplay between physiological domains is hypothesized to be a primary determinant of system resilience.
source: Thus far we had examined how individual features change with age, but because the interplay between physiological domains is hypothesized to be a primary determinant of system resilience (Cohen, 2016), we were also interested in the connectivity between these features and how that connectivity changes with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The study fit a graphical model (a semi-parametric Gaussian copula model) using sparse precision matrix estimation methods and visualized the model as a force-directed network.
source: More precisely, we fit a graphical model (a semi-parametric Gaussian copula model) using sparse precision matrix estimation methods and visualized the model as a force-directed network (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Consensus clustering resulted in 22 clusters.
source: We determined the number of clusters and clustering of features via consensus clustering, which resulted in 22 clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the clustering analysis.

claim: Ratio-based features, state-conditioned features, and time-of-day conditioned features often clustered separately from one another, demonstrating that different data aggregation approaches convey different information.
source: Ratio-based features, state-conditioned features, and time-of-day conditioned features often clustered separately from one another; this demonstrates that different data aggregation approaches convey different information.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with inference from clustering results.

claim: Nodes within a cluster share similar physiological underpinnings rather than simply similar sensor hardware.
source: Furthermore, this suggests that nodes within a cluster share similar physiological underpinnings rather than simply similar sensor hardware.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from clustering results.

claim: Body mass was one of the most well-defined and least-connected clusters, largely independent of other clusters.
source: One of the most well-defined and least-connected clusters was body mass, as demonstrated by its small arc radius: all body mass metrics formed a tight cluster that was largely independent of other clusters.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing network connectivity patterns.

claim: The low connectivity of body mass to other phenotype clusters demonstrates that variance in body mass does not drive all, or even most, of the variance in other features in this dataset.
source: The low connectivity of body mass to other phenotype clusters demonstrates that variance in body mass does not drive all, or even most, of the variance in other features in this dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from network analysis.

claim: Metabolic rate and high activity pattern were the most densely connected clusters, indicating that these physiological characteristics impact (or are impacted by) many other physiological domains.
source: In contrast, metabolic rate and high activity pattern were the most densely connected clusters, indicating that these physiological characteristics impact (or are impacted by) many other physiological domains.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing network connectivity patterns.

claim: Resilience refers to the ability of a system to maintain function in the face of change.
source: Resilience refers to the ability of a system to maintain function in the face of change.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section defining resilience.

claim: In a resilient system, a small disruption in one physiological domain will have limited system-wide effect, whereas in a less resilient system, the same perturbation will affect more of the network.
source: In a resilient system, a small disruption in one physiological domain will have limited system-wide effect, whereas in a less resilient system, the same perturbation will affect more of the network.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section explaining the concept of resilience.

claim: In less resilient systems, individual subsystems (nodes) are sensitive to the fluctuations of other subsystems, leading to a rising correlation between subsystems.
source: Thus, in less resilient systems, individual subsystems (nodes) are sensitive to the fluctuations of other subsystems, leading to a rising correlation between subsystems (Scheffer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Visual inspection of per-age networks from 3 to 6 months to 33+ months suggested increasing connectivity with time, suggesting decreasing system resilience.
source: Visual inspection of these per-age networks from 3 to 6 months to 33+ months suggested increasing connectivity with time, suggesting decreasing system resilience.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing visual observations of network changes.

claim: Resilience (negative multivariate mutual information) exhibited a striking decrease with age, with an accelerating rate of decline.
source: Resilience (negative MI) exhibited a striking decrease with age, with an accelerating rate of decline; this pattern qualitatively reflects the accelerating failure rate associated with aging better than the semi-linear or early-life dropoff we observed with many individual parameters in this study (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Resilience may be more accurate representations of physiological aging than are individual features.
source: Thus, resilience may be more accurate representations of physiological aging than are individual features.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from resilience analysis.

claim: Inter-cluster resilience exhibited a striking decrease with age, suggesting the connectivity between subsystems increases with age.
source: Like overall resilience, inter-cluster resilience exhibited a striking decrease with age (Figure 3E), suggesting the connectivity between subsystems increases with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Increased connectivity with age was observed for the majority of clusters.
source: This effect was not merely driven by a few outlying clusters; increased connectivity with age was observed for the majority of clusters (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Most clusters showed a decline in intra-cluster resilience with age (increasing connectivity), but trajectories varied.
source: Most clusters showed a decline in resilience with age (increasing connectivity), but trajectories varied: some clusters exhibited a nearly linear decline in resilience, whereas others exhibited a late-life acceleration, perhaps indicating that certain domains of physiology are more prone to a loss of resilience with age than others.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing intra-cluster resilience patterns.

claim: An increasingly common approach when dealing with multi-dimensional aging data is to train models that predict relevant endpoints (aging 'clocks').
source: An increasingly common approach when dealing with multi-dimensional aging data is to train models that predict relevant endpoints (so-called aging 'clocks').
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing current approaches to biological age prediction.

claim: Previous studies have developed models that predict either chronological age or mortality risk separately, but neither chronological age nor mortality risk fully encapsulates an individual's multi-system, aging-related health status (biological age).
source: These studies have developed models that predict either chronological age or mortality risk separately, but these separate approaches are limited because neither chronological age nor mortality risk fully encapsulates an individual's multi-system, aging-related health status, that is, biological age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section critiquing existing approaches.

claim: The study developed an aging rate regression model (CASPAR) in which biological age is determined from a combination of chronological age and health status (time to death).
source: To address this, we developed an aging rate regression model in which biological age is determined from a combination of chronological age and health status (in this case, time to death, though other health proxies such as a frailty score could be used).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the CASPAR model.

claim: The CASPAR model includes a hyperparameter (σ_β) that allows for tuning of the relative weighting of chronological age and time to death.
source: The model includes a hyperparameter that allows for tuning of the relative weighting of chronological age and time to death, allowing us to generate models with different behaviors.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the CASPAR model.

claim: Chronological age and time to death are not particularly well correlated with one another.
source: Neither chronological age nor time to death are perfect representations of aging rate, and they are not particularly well correlated with one another (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), thus optimizing the prediction of one necessarily reduces performance for the other, resulting in a tunable tension in model behavior and the ability to explore intermediate states that may avoid overfitting to either of these imperfect biological age surrogates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The balanced prediction of both dimensions by the hybrid model suggests that it may represent a qualitatively different approach to quantifying health-relevant biological age than either age or survival prediction alone.
source: This balanced prediction of both dimensions suggests that the hybrid model may represent a qualitatively different approach to quantifying health-relevant biological age than either age or survival prediction alone.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion about the hybrid model.

claim: For all three model classes (age, time to death, and hybrid), the top 20 most informative features came from multiple clusters and sensors and aggregation methods, with no single cluster or sensor dominating.
source: For all three model classes (age, time to death, and hybrid), the top 20 most informative features came from multiple clusters and sensors (gas, photobeams, wheel, body mass) and aggregation methods (state-conditioned, time of day, lights on/off ratio) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C). No single cluster or sensor dominated, demonstrating the importance of a high-dimensional feature set.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and 1C.

claim: Of the top 20 features from each model, 7 were shared across all three model classes.
source: Of the top 20 features from each model, 7 were shared across all three (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Features shared across all three models include major aspects of physiology – overall size (BodyMass), activity (wheel running and pedestrian locomotion), and a surrogate of basal metabolic rate (VCO2 while Sleeping).
source: Perhaps unsurprisingly, these include major aspects of physiology – overall size (BodyMass), activity (wheel running and pedestrian locomotion), and a surrogate of basal metabolic rate (VCO2 while Sleeping).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing shared features.

claim: Features more associated with time to death than with age include measures of activity during the light phase or low activity states, perhaps indicating that a breakdown in circadian stability is an indicator of impending demise.
source: Features more associated with time to death than with age ('TTD and Hybrid only' and 'TTD only') include measures of activity (wheel, food, and water intake) during the light phase or low activity states, perhaps indicating that a breakdown in circadian stability is an indicator of impending demise.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with inference about feature meaning.

claim: Features more associated with age than time to death include the extent of activity during the dark phase, perhaps indicating that the best predictor of chronological age is a decline in high intensity activity.
source: Conversely, features more associated with age than time to death ('Age only') include the extent of activity during the dark phase, perhaps indicating that the best predictor of chronological age is a decline in high intensity activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with inference about feature meaning.

claim: Limited overlap between age and mortality prediction models has been reported elsewhere using different measures of physiological age.
source: Limited overlap between age and mortality prediction models has been reported elsewhere using different measures of physiological age (Schultz et al., 2020), thus this may represent a more general truth about organism-level aging: aging-related changes in physiological function, though of clear health relevance to the individual, are only partially related to mortality risk, demonstrating the need for a thoughtful balance between these conceptualizations of biological age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Aging-related changes in physiological function, though of clear health relevance to the individual, are only partially related to mortality risk, demonstrating the need for a thoughtful balance between these conceptualizations of biological age.
source: Limited overlap between age and mortality prediction models has been reported elsewhere using different measures of physiological age (Schultz et al., 2020), thus this may represent a more general truth about organism-level aging: aging-related changes in physiological function, though of clear health relevance to the individual, are only partially related to mortality risk, demonstrating the need for a thoughtful balance between these conceptualizations of biological age.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion.

claim: The study advances the state of the art for healthspan assessment in terms of throughput, resolution, and physiological scope.
source: This study advances the state of the art for healthspan assessment in terms of throughput, resolution, and physiological scope.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of contributions.

claim: At the outset of this study, it was not clear that monitoring of mice in a normal living environment would provide sufficient sensitivity to detect age-related changes.
source: At the outset of this study, it was not clear that monitoring of mice in a normal living environment would provide sufficient sensitivity to detect age-related changes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section reflecting on initial uncertainty.

claim: The data show a plethora of aging-related changes in all age groups, including prior to 6 months of age, demonstrating that automated phenotyping of voluntary activity can detect even early aging-related changes.
source: Although some aspects of aging undoubtedly require such assays, we found that our data show a plethora of aging-related changes in all age groups, including prior to 6 months of age, demonstrating that automated phenotyping of voluntary activity can detect even early aging-related changes.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a key finding.

claim: Mice reach sexual maturity at ~6 weeks of age, but are arguably still undergoing developmental changes for weeks or months after that.
source: Mice reach sexual maturity at ~6 weeks of age, but are arguably still undergoing developmental changes for weeks or months after that.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as background knowledge.

claim: Phenotypes which change monotonically, particularly when the trajectory is linear, can be considered part of aging even when that change begins early.
source: However, we did notice that phenotypes exhibited a diversity of trajectories across life – unchanged, parabolic, linear, logarithmic, and nearly exponential – and we propose that phenotypes which change monotonically, particularly when the trajectory is linear, can be considered part of aging even when that change begins early.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal.

claim: Wheel running declines near-monotonically with age starting at 3 months, which can reasonably be considered an aspect of aging that begins quite early.
source: For example, wheel running declines near-monotonically with age starting at 3 months; it seems reasonable to propose that this is an aspect of aging that begins quite early.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an example.

claim: The study developed a robust HMM to assign a behavioral state to each 3 min time bin to distinguish changes in physiology from changes in behavior.
source: To address this, we developed a robust HMM to assign a behavioral state to each 3 min time bin.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing methodology.

claim: State-conditioned features arising from the same sensor often clustered separately from one another, indicating that they contained complementary physiological information.
source: This turned out to be an informative approach, as state-conditioned features arising from the same sensor often clustered separately from one another, indicating that they contained complementary physiological information (e.g., pedestrian locomotion while eating versus while resting).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing findings.

claim: Energy expenditure while sleeping provides a reasonable surrogate of resting metabolic rate whereas VO2 while running provides a reasonable surrogate of maximal oxygen consumption, both of which decline with age.
source: For example, energy expenditure while sleeping provides a reasonable surrogate of resting metabolic rate whereas VO2 while running provides a reasonable surrogate of maximal oxygen consumption, both of which decline with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing physiological interpretations.

claim: Behavioral inference based on automated phenotyping data is a useful technique that can be applied in a number of preclinical contexts.
source: We propose that behavioral inference based on automated phenotyping data is a useful technique that can be applied in a number of preclinical contexts.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a proposal.

claim: The study built a network of physiological and behavioral phenotypes using sparse precision matrix estimation methods to determine every pairwise correlation between features after accounting for all other features.
source: We built a network of physiological and behavioral phenotypes using sparse precision matrix estimation methods; in other words, we determined every pairwise correlation between features after accounting for all other features.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing methodology.

claim: Two features connected by a strong edge (high covariance) are more likely to be mechanistically connected than two features with a weaker edge.
source: In this context, two features connected by a strong edge (high covariance) are more likely to be mechanistically connected than two features with a weaker edge, and thus features that form a cluster are likely driven by the same mechanism(s), whereas features from a different cluster are likely driven by distinct mechanism(s).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section explaining network interpretation.

claim: The study identified 22 distinct organism-level clusters, though this number will undoubtedly be refined as additional studies are incorporated into the network analysis framework.
source: In this study, we identified 22 distinct organism-level clusters, though this number will undoubtedly be refined as additional studies are incorporated into the network analysis framework.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing findings.

claim: More than virtually any individual feature, resilience smoothly and monotonically declined with age, decreasing more rapidly in old animals than in young animals.
source: We uncovered striking changes with age in this dimension: more than virtually any individual feature, resilience smoothly and monotonically declined with age. The decline in resilience accelerated with age, decreasing more rapidly in old animals than in young animals, a pattern that is qualitatively consistent with the accelerating decline in health and corresponding exponential increase in mortality with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing resilience findings.

claim: The decline in resilience accelerated with age, a pattern qualitatively consistent with the accelerating decline in health and corresponding exponential increase in mortality with age.
source: The decline in resilience accelerated with age, decreasing more rapidly in old animals than in young animals, a pattern that is qualitatively consistent with the accelerating decline in health and corresponding exponential increase in mortality with age.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing resilience findings.

claim: This emergent property of the system (resilience) was only detectable by analyzing the relationship between phenotypes, rather than the individual values of the phenotypes themselves.
source: This emergent property of the system was only detectable by analyzing the relationship between phenotypes, rather than the individual values of the phenotypes themselves – an analytical approach that is infeasible for data from challenge-based assays.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section emphasizing the unique capability of the approach.

claim: Increasing network connectivity indicates that, with age, runs increasingly resemble one another, that is, old animals occupy a lower diversity of phenotypic states than younger animals.
source: Increasing network connectivity indicates that, with age, runs increasingly resemble one another, that is, old animals occupy a lower diversity of phenotypic states than younger animals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section interpreting network connectivity findings.

claim: A similar phenomenon has been reported for human frailty – inter-individual variation in frailty scores decreases with age.
source: A similar phenomenon has been reported for human frailty – inter-individual variation in frailty scores decreases with age (Rockwood et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a supporting citation.

claim: It is unclear how much error is optimal in age prediction models; that is, it is unclear whether the error should be 1%, 5%, 20%, or more.
source: However, although it is clear that perfect performance is not desirable, it is unclear how much error is optimal; that is, it is unclear whether the error should be 1%, 5%, 20%, or more.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section critiquing existing approaches.

claim: The desire for error is not explicitly stated during model training – algorithms push toward perfect performance whenever possible and do not aim to capture any other type of information.
source: Further, the desire for error is not explicitly stated during model training – algorithms push toward perfect performance whenever possible and do not aim to capture any other type of information.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section critiquing existing approaches.

claim: Survival time is objectively measurable and fulfills the criteria of being independent of the training data, but it is still not exactly what we care about from an aging perspective: not all individuals with equal remaining lifespan are equally healthy or equally 'aged'.
source: Survival time is objectively measurable and fulfills the criteria of being independent of the training data, but it is still not exactly what we care about from an aging perspective: not all individuals with equal remaining lifespan are equally healthy or equally 'aged'.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section critiquing survival time as an outcome.

claim: Lifespan is influenced by a large number of external factors, and mortality risk is often dominated by particular pathologies (e.g., cancer, in the case of many mouse strains).
source: Lifespan is influenced by a large number of external factors, and mortality risk is often dominated by particular pathologies (e.g., cancer, in the case of many mouse strains).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section discussing limitations of lifespan as an outcome.

claim: An anti-cancer drug or any other single-cause-of-death modulator does not meet most people's criteria of an aging intervention, but would be viewed as such if survival time were the single outcome variable assessed.
source: An anti-cancer drug or any other single-cause-of-death modulator does not meet most people's criteria of an aging intervention, but would be viewed as such if survival time were the single outcome variable assessed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section critiquing survival time as the sole outcome.

claim: CASPAR explicitly captures two key notions: (1) biological age should be correlated to chronological age and (2) deviations of biological age from chronological age should be informative of some proxy of health status (e.g., time to death).
source: CASPAR explicitly captures two key notions: (1) biological age should be correlated to chronological age and (2) deviations of biological age from chronological age should be informative of some proxy of health status (e.g., time to death).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing the CASPAR approach.

claim: Age prediction was always more accurate than survival time prediction, but this is not surprising – the former is an exercise in estimating a concurrent variable (chronological age), whereas the latter predicts a future outcome that is dependent on a number of stochastic external influences.
source: Age prediction was always more accurate than survival time prediction, but this is not surprising – the former is an exercise in estimating a concurrent variable (chronological age), whereas the latter predicts a future outcome that is dependent on a number of stochastic external influences that have not yet occurred and may have no relationship to an animal's current state.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section explaining model performance differences.

claim: Both age and mortality information are present in the data, but the feature weighting that predicts them is largely distinct.
source: Therefore, both age and mortality information are present in the data, but the feature weighting that predicts them is largely distinct.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing model findings.

claim: A similar dichotomy between age and survival time prediction has been reported in other physiological datasets.
source: A similar dichotomy between age and survival time prediction has been reported in other physiological datasets (Schultz et al., 2020; Fischer et al., 2016; Levine et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: Considerable thought must go into model design, as different outcome variables are likely to emphasize different aspects of biology.
source: Thus, considerable thought must go into model design, as different outcome variables are likely to emphasize different aspects of biology.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a conclusion.

claim: Predicted biological age from the hybrid model was more strongly correlated to time to death than chronological age itself.
source: Notably, predicted biological age from the hybrid model was more strongly correlated to time to death than chronological age itself.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing hybrid model performance.

claim: Hybrid models are likely to be more valuable and aging-relevant than either extreme (pure age or pure survival models).
source: It is beyond the scope of this manuscript to dictate exactly where the age versus survival prediction trade-off should lie, but we hypothesize that such hybrid models are likely to be more valuable and aging-relevant than either extreme.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis.

claim: The CASPAR approach can be applied more broadly to any other high-dimensional, per-individual dataset, including methylation data, transcriptomic data, and blood biomarkers.
source: The model framework we have developed, with the ability to tune the relative weighting of age and survival time, can be applied more broadly. First, the underlying data does not need to be physiological. A similar approach can be used with any other high-dimensional, per-individual dataset, including methylation data, transcriptomic data, and blood biomarkers.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing broader applications.

claim: For the purposes of preclinical intervention testing, physiological data is favored because it is, almost by definition, health-relevant.
source: For the purposes of preclinical intervention testing, we favor physiological data because it is, almost by definition, health-relevant.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section explaining the choice of data type.

claim: Physiological data-based models relied on features like body mass, running speed, energy expenditure, and sleeping behavior, which is intuitively sensible and provides confidence that the resulting model truly reflects animal function.
source: Our models relied on features like body mass, running speed, energy expenditure, and sleeping behavior – this is intuitively sensible and provides confidence that the resulting model truly reflects animal function.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section explaining the advantage of physiological data.

claim: Molecular data is often easier to acquire and contains more features, but there is limited prior information on each individual feature, meaning that molecular data-based models are more difficult to interpret and sanity check.
source: In contrast, although molecular data is often easier to acquire and contains more features, there is limited prior information on each individual feature, meaning that molecular data-based models are more difficult to interpret and sanity check.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section comparing data types.

claim: The CASPAR modeling framework can use an outcome variable other than death, such as a morbidity endpoint or a pre-determined 'health score', which may be particularly useful in human datasets where follow-up mortality data is often limited.
source: A second way to broaden the application of this modeling framework is by using an outcome variable other than death. This may be particularly useful in human datasets, where follow-up mortality data is often limited. Age could be combined with a moribidity endpoint, or a pre-determined 'health score', and these outcome variables could be used to train the model.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section describing broader applications.

claim: The study is not a fully longitudinal design; mice were enrolled starting at different ages and followed for a fixed length of time (~1.5 years), thus the data are both left-truncated and right-censored.
source: First, it is not a fully longitudinal design. Mice were enrolled starting at different ages and followed for a fixed length of time (~1.5 years), thus our data are both left-truncated and right-censored.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: The cohort was entirely female, which was a practical necessity due to the aggressive tendencies of DO males requiring single housing.
source: Second, the cohort was entirely female. This was a practical necessity; due to their aggressive tendencies, DO males are generally singly housed at all times, leading to unsustainable financial and vivarium space requirements.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: A mixed dataset would be preferable, not only in terms of sex, but also in terms of strain and environmental variables, because mixed datasets increase the generalizability of conclusions.
source: Nevertheless, a mixed dataset would be preferable, not only in terms of sex, but also in terms of strain and environmental variables, because mixed datasets increase the generalizability of conclusions (Voelkl et al., 2020, Webster and Rutz, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with supporting citations.

claim: It is quite likely that the specific physiological changes that develop with age will differ in male mice, in other strains, and in animals housed under different conditions.
source: It is quite likely that the specific physiological changes that develop with age will differ in male mice, in other strains, and in animals housed under different conditions; however, we suspect that broad patterns such as reduced wheel running, metabolic activity, and resilience, will generalize.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section discussing generalizability.

claim: Broad patterns such as reduced wheel running, metabolic activity, and resilience are suspected to generalize across sex, strain, and environmental conditions.
source: It is quite likely that the specific physiological changes that develop with age will differ in male mice, in other strains, and in animals housed under different conditions; however, we suspect that broad patterns such as reduced wheel running, metabolic activity, and resilience, will generalize.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a hypothesis about generalizability.

claim: Although the automated monitoring cages provided a tremendous amount of data, they are blind to many health-relevant phenotypes such as body posture and coat condition.
source: Additionally, although the automated monitoring cages we used provided a tremendous amount of data, they are blind to many health-relevant phenotypes such as body posture and coat condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: Additional high content, automated phenotyping modalities, such as video monitoring paired with machine vision feature extraction, would increase the value of this platform.
source: Additional high content, automated phenotyping modalities, such as video monitoring paired with machine vision feature extraction, would increase the value of this platform.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a potential improvement.

claim: The most granular analyses used 3 min time windows, but for many of the cage sensors, the data are acquired every second, providing the opportunity for more sophisticated time series analyses.
